implementation_notes: No language supports or suppresses this; the toolchain does. The procedure that avoids the smell is a fixed order of operations: write the performance requirement (latency, throughput, memory, battery, deadline), establish a baseline measurement, find where the time actually goes, and only then optimise that place. The two activities that are commonly conflated are worth separating explicitly. Choosing the right algorithm and data structure is design work and belongs in the first phase — an O(n log n) sort instead of an O(n^2) one, a map instead of a linear scan, a streaming layout instead of an in-memory one. Hand-tuning the implementation of code you have not measured is the other kind, and it is the premature one. The rule's operative clause is the second half of the quotation: look carefully at the critical code, but only after it has been identified.
idiom_name: profile-then-optimise; the rule is 'identify the critical code', not 'never optimise'
code_sketch:
# the order of operations, not a prohibition
1. requirement: 50k rows/s, p99 < 40ms        # written down, or there is nothing to meet
2. baseline:   p99 = 380ms (measured)
3. profile:    340ms in the O(n^2) merge, not in the parser
4. optimise:   replace with a hash join -> p99 = 22ms
# unmeasured: replacing the stdlib sort with a hand-rolled one. Nobody knows.
pitfalls: Quoting the truncated maxim and concluding that performance is never a design concern, which produces systems that need rewriting.
Micro-optimising what the compiler already handles, and then reading that back as the reason the optimisation was pointless.
Optimising a prototype, so the complexity is written against a structure that will not survive.
Optimising where the code is being written rather than at the I/O boundary, lock or allocation site where the time actually is.
